readerTitle: The $12,000 argument two co-founders never had
caseNote: 가상 사례 (집수리 회사, 일정 관리 앱) + 실제 연구 (Jehn의 갈등 유형 연구, de Wit·Greer·Jehn 2012 메타분석) · 수치는 설명용
insight: 공동창업자 갈등의 진짜 비용은 다툼 자체가 아니라, 미뤄진 업무 갈등이 사람에 대한 불만으로 바뀌는 데서 나온다.
misconception: 좋은 공동창업자 관계는 싸우지 않는 관계다. 불편한 주제를 피하면 관계가 지켜진다.

sources.text: Jehn, K. A. (1995). A multimethod examination of the benefits and detriments of intragroup conflict. Administrative Science Quarterly, 40(2).
de Wit, F. R. C., Greer, L. L., & Jehn, K. A. (2012). The paradox of intragroup conflict: A meta-analysis. Journal of Applied Psychology, 97(2), 360–390.
Simons, T. L., & Peterson, R. S. (2000). Task conflict and relationship conflict in top management teams: The pivotal role of intragroup trust. Journal of Applied Psychology, 85(1).
집수리 회사와 앱 사례의 모든 수치는 설명용 가상 예시

factChecks.note: 계산 확인: 작업당 가격 차이 $20 × 월 100건 × 6개월 = $12,000. '기존 고객 대부분이 인상된 가격에도 남는다'는 가정 위의 수치이며, 카드 본문에 이 가정을 밝혔습니다.
de Wit 외(2012) 메타분석 결과 요약 확인 필요: 관계 갈등은 팀 성과와 일관되게 부정적 관계, 업무 갈등은 전체적으로 뚜렷한 부정적 관계가 없고 최고경영진 팀 등 일부 조건에서 긍정적 관계. 카드에는 연구 수·표본 수를 넣지 않았습니다.
Simons & Peterson(2000): 신뢰가 낮을 때 업무 갈등이 관계 갈등으로 번지기 쉽다는 결과. 카드 7의 '신뢰가 있을 때만 도움이 된다'는 표현이 원문 결론과 맞는지 확인하세요.

cards.title: The $12,000 argument two co-founders never had
body: Ana and Leo run a small home repair company together. They're old friends. They never raise their voices. In six months, they haven't had a single argument.
That calm cost them about $12,000. And it nearly cost them the friendship.

image.label: Two co-founders smiling politely with a growing pile of coins slipping away behind them
image.brief: 3D 클레이 스타일. 작업복 차림의 공동창업자 두 명이 공구 상자를 사이에 두고 어색하게 웃고 있음. 두 사람 뒤로 동전이 조금씩 새어 나가는 구멍 난 저금통. 실제 로고나 상표는 쓰지 않음.

cards.title: Your co-founder keeps changing the subject.
body: You're Ana. You think your prices are too low: rivals charge about $20 more per job. Leo worries higher prices will scare off regular customers.
You've hinted at it twice. Both times Leo changed the subject. It's a busy month. What do you do?

options.text: Wait until the busy season ends so it doesn't add stress
options.feedback: You keep the peace this month. But the low price runs on every job while you wait, and your frustration grows quietly.

options.text: Put it on this week's agenda and propose a test: quote new jobs at the higher price for four weeks, then compare
options.feedback: You turn a clash of opinions into a question the numbers can answer. The cost is one uncomfortable meeting.

options.text: Let Leo have the final say, since he talks to customers
options.feedback: This ends the delay, which helps. But giving in without being heard pushes the disagreement underground, and it tends to return in another form.

cards.title: What six quiet months cost.

breakdown.label: Jobs a month
breakdown.detail: Every one at the old price

breakdown.label: Money not earned
breakdown.detail: If most customers would have stayed

cards.callout: The bigger cost came later. By month six, Ana no longer thought Leo was wrong about prices. She thought **he didn't listen**.

cards.title: Two kinds of founder conflict
body: **Task conflict** is disagreement about the work: prices, hires, which customers to chase.
**Relationship conflict** is friction about each other: trust, fairness, respect.
The twist: a task conflict handled in the open is often useful. Left unspoken, it tends to turn into a relationship conflict. Ana's pricing question became a story about Leo as a person.

image.label: A disagreement about a price tag turning into two people facing away from each other
image.brief: 왼쪽에서 오른쪽으로 흐르는 3단 그림. 1단: 두 사람이 가격표 하나를 함께 보며 의견을 나눔("Task"). 2단: 가격표 위에 먼지가 쌓이고 둘 사이가 멀어짐. 3단: 두 사람이 등을 돌림("Relationship"). 실제 로고 없음.

cards.title: Research treats the two very differently.
body: In the 1990s, management researcher Karen Jehn showed that teams experience these two kinds of conflict separately.

A 2012 meta-analysis by de Wit, Greer and Jehn combined many studies of team conflict. Relationship conflict was consistently linked to worse team performance. Task conflict was not consistently harmful, and in some settings, such as senior leadership teams, it went with better results.
Disagreeing about the work is not the danger. Letting it become personal is.

cards.title: Keep the fight about the work.
body: A few habits keep task conflict from turning personal:
list: **Name the issue, not the person:** "Our prices are low," not "You never listen"
**Give hard topics a fixed slot** in a regular founder meeting
**Turn opinions into tests** with a deadline
**Agree how a tie is broken** before you need it
cards.callout: The goal isn't less disagreement. It's faster disagreement.

cards.title: Not every conflict can be tested away.
body: Task conflict helps mostly when trust is already there. Research on leadership teams suggests that where trust is low, debates about the work are more likely to be heard as personal attacks.

And some disagreements are about values, not tactics. If one founder wants a calm lifestyle business and the other wants to grow fast, no four-week test will settle it. That may call for a new agreement, or a planned split.

cards.title: Now it's a software company.
body: You're the CEO of a small scheduling app. Your CTO co-founder wants to spend next quarter rebuilding old code. You want to ship features a big customer asked for.
In the meeting, the CTO snaps: "You always choose customers over keeping the product alive." What do you say?

options.text: "That's unfair. You always want to play with the tech."
options.feedback: It feels like defending yourself. But now you're both arguing about each other, and the roadmap question gets lost.

options.text: "Let's separate this. Can we each list what our plan costs and risks, and decide by Friday?"
options.feedback: You pull the conflict back to the work and set a deadline. The CTO's concern gets a fair hearing without you accepting the personal charge.
The tension drops today, and the rebuild may even be right. But the customer question stays unanswered, and you may start resenting the decision.

cards.title: Argue about the work early, so you never argue about each other.
body: Avoided disagreements don't disappear. They keep costing money, and they slowly turn into doubts about your partner.
**Try it today:** write down one topic you and a partner or colleague keep stepping around. Propose a time this week to discuss it, framed as a question you can test.
